items.prompt: Which expression gives the absolute pressure at depth h in a static fluid of density rho, where P0 is the pressure at the surface?

options.label: P0 + rho g h
P0 + rho g / h
P0 - rho g h
P0 + rho v^2 h

rubric: Pressure in a static fluid increases linearly with depth: P = P0 + rho g h.
Distractors flip the sign, divide by depth, or wrongly bring in velocity.

items.prompt: What is the SI unit of pressure?

options.label: Joule (N m)
Watt (J/s)
Pascal (N/m^2)
Newton (kg m/s^2)

rubric: Pressure is force per unit area, so its SI unit is the pascal, 1 N/m^2.
Distractors are units of force, energy and power.

items.prompt: Which equation expresses the continuity equation for steady incompressible flow through a pipe with cross-sectional area A and mean speed v?

options.label: A1 v1 = A2 v2
P1 v1 = P2 v2

rubric: Volume flow rate A v is constant for steady incompressible flow.
Distractors use a ratio, pressure, or a sum, none of which conserve flow rate.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly gives Archimedes' principle?

options.label: The buoyant force equals the weight of the object submerged
The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid it displaces
The buoyant force equals the pressure on the top surface alone
The buoyant force equals the object's volume times its density

rubric: Buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid.
Distractors confuse it with the object's own weight, its mass, or a single surface pressure.

items.prompt: What does the term viscosity describe for a fluid?

options.label: Its tendency to change volume when pressure is applied
Its ability to climb narrow tubes through surface forces
Its mass per unit volume at a given temperature
Its resistance to flow from internal friction between layers

rubric: Viscosity is internal resistance to shear or flow.
Distractors describe density, compressibility and capillarity.

items.prompt: Which quantities appear as terms in Bernoulli's equation for steady, incompressible, frictionless flow? Select all that apply.

options.label: Surface tension coefficient
Hydrostatic term rho g h
Dynamic pressure 1/2 rho v^2
Viscous stress mu times velocity gradient
Static pressure P

rubric: Bernoulli's equation sums pressure, kinetic and potential terms per unit volume.
Viscous stress and surface tension are not part of the ideal equation.

items.prompt: An engineer calculates a Reynolds number of 1200 for water flowing through a smooth circular pipe. She recalls the standard rule of thumb that separates the flow regimes in pipes. Which regime does this value indicate?

options.label: Choked flow
Cavitating flow
Laminar flow
Turbulent flow

rubric: In pipes, Re below about 2300 is conventionally laminar.
Turbulent is the choice if the threshold is misremembered; choked and cavitating flow are unrelated to Re thresholds.

items.prompt: Why does the pressure in a still lake increase as you go deeper?

options.label: Water at depth is heavily compressed so it becomes far denser
Pressure acts only downward so it keeps adding up with depth
Water molecules move much faster at greater depths
The water at depth must support the weight of more water above

rubric: Pressure grows because deeper fluid supports the weight of the column above it.
Distractors invoke big density change, molecular speed, or a downward-only pressure.

items.prompt: Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows to half its original cross-sectional area. How does the water's speed in the narrow section compare with the wide section?

options.label: It is halved
It is unchanged
It is quadrupled
It is doubled

rubric: Continuity A v = constant, so halving area doubles speed.
Halved reflects inverting the relation; unchanged ignores continuity.

items.prompt: Air moves faster over the top of a wing than under it. Using Bernoulli's equation along streamlines, how is the pressure above the wing predicted to compare with below?

options.label: Higher, because faster air carries more thermal energy
Lower, because higher speed goes with lower pressure
Higher, because faster air pushes harder on the surface
The same, because air pressure is always atmospheric

rubric: Along a streamline, higher speed corresponds to lower static pressure.
Distractors assume faster flow pushes harder or ignore pressure differences.

items.prompt: A solid block has a density of 600 kg/m^3 and is placed in fresh water (1000 kg/m^3). What happens, and why?

options.label: It sinks, because solids are normally denser than liquids
It floats, because its mass is small compared to the water
It floats, because its density is less than the water's
It sinks, because its weight always acts downward on it

rubric: An object floats when its average density is below the fluid's.
Distractors confuse mass with density or use a false rule about solids.

items.prompt: In an ideal hydraulic lift, the output piston has 10 times the area of the input piston. Compared with the force on the input piston, the force the output piston can exert is:

options.label: 10 times larger
10 times smaller
Equal
100 times larger

rubric: Pascal's principle gives equal pressure, so force scales with area: 10 times.
Distractors invert the ratio, ignore area, or square it.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe turbulent flow compared with laminar flow in a pipe? Select all that apply.

options.label: Friction losses are typically larger
Fluid moves in chaotic, mixing eddies
It occurs at higher Reynolds numbers
Fluid layers slide smoothly without mixing
It occurs only in gases, never in liquids

rubric: Turbulence is eddying, appears at high Re and increases losses.
Smooth layers describe laminar flow; liquids can be turbulent too.

items.prompt: A cargo ship with a fixed load sails from a freshwater river into the open sea. Seawater is denser than river water. How does the ship's draft change, and why?

options.label: It sits lower, because saltier water is heavier to push through
It sits higher, because less displaced volume balances its weight
It sits higher, because the buoyant force on it increases
It sits the same, because the ship's weight is unchanged

rubric: Buoyant force must equal the unchanged weight, so denser fluid needs less displaced volume.
Distractors claim the buoyant force changes or that weight alone fixes the draft.

items.prompt: Three open vertical tubes of different widths are joined at their bases and filled with water that is at rest. How do the water levels in the tubes compare?

options.label: Highest in the widest tube, because it holds more water pushing down
Lowest in the widest tube, because its weight spreads over more area
Highest in the narrowest tube, because the water is squeezed upward more
All at the same height, because pressure depends on depth, not tube width

rubric: In a connected static fluid, pressure is equal at equal depth, so the free surfaces sit at the same height.
Distractors confuse pressure with total weight or tube width.

items.prompt: Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows. How does the speed in the narrow section compare with the wide section?

options.label: Smaller, because pressure is higher there and holds the water back
The same, because incompressible water cannot change its speed
Greater, because the same volume per second must pass through less area
Smaller, because friction with the walls is larger in narrow sections

rubric: Continuity: A1v1 = A2v2 for incompressible steady flow, so smaller area means higher speed.
Distractors rely on friction or pressure intuition rather than conservation of volume flow.

items.prompt: In steady, horizontal flow of an ideal fluid along a streamline, what happens to pressure where the fluid speed is higher?

options.label: It is higher, since faster fluid pushes harder on its surroundings
It is higher, since moving fluid has more momentum to transfer
It is lower, since kinetic energy per volume rises as pressure falls
It is unchanged, since pressure depends only on height here

rubric: Bernoulli: p + 0.5*rho*v^2 stays constant at constant height, so higher speed means lower pressure.
Distractors link speed to greater push or ignore the energy exchange.

items.prompt: A mechanic warms motor oil from 20 C to 80 C. What happens to its viscosity?

options.label: It increases, because the warmed oil expands and becomes denser
It decreases, because molecular attractions weaken and layers slide more easily
It stays constant, because viscosity is a fixed property of the oil
It increases, because faster molecules collide more and resist sliding

rubric: Liquid viscosity falls as temperature rises because intermolecular cohesion weakens.
Distractors borrow gas behaviour or assume viscosity is fixed.

items.prompt: A steel ship floats even though steel is denser than water. What best explains this?

options.label: Steel becomes less dense than water once it is shaped into a hull
Its average density, counting the air inside the hull, is below water's
Surface tension of the water holds the heavy hull up at the surface
Water pressure under the hull always exceeds the weight of the steel

rubric: A body floats when its overall average density is below the fluid's, so displaced water weight equals ship weight.
Distractors claim density changes with shape or invoke surface tension or pressure alone.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe laminar flow in a circular pipe? Select all that apply.

options.label: Eddies continually mix fluid across the layers
It occurs at low Reynolds number
The velocity profile across the pipe is parabolic
Speed is the same at the wall as at the centre
Fluid moves in smooth, parallel layers

rubric: Laminar flow is layered, occurs at low Re and gives a parabolic profile.
Eddy mixing describes turbulence, and the wall speed is zero (no-slip).

items.prompt: A gardener holds a thumb over part of a hose opening and notices the water jet shoots much farther. The tap setting has not changed, so the volume of water leaving per second is about the same. Which explanation is best?

options.label: The smaller opening lowers the water density, so the water speeds up
The smaller opening forces the same flow through less area, so exit speed rises
The thumb reduces friction inside the hose, so the water speeds up
The thumb adds pressure energy to the water, so the water speed rises

rubric: Continuity: with Q fixed, smaller exit area means higher speed.
Distractors invent energy input, friction reduction or density change.

items.prompt: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 10 m in fresh water (density 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.81 m/s^2)?

options.label: 9.8 kPa
981 kPa
199 kPa
98 kPa

rubric: 199 kPa is absolute pressure including atmosphere; others are power-of-ten slips.

items.prompt: Water at 2 m/s flows in a 10 cm diameter pipe that narrows to 5 cm diameter. What is the speed in the narrow section?

options.label: 8 m/s
16 m/s
2 m/s
4 m/s

rubric: Area scales with diameter squared, so halving the diameter quarters the area and quadruples speed: 8 m/s.
4 m/s uses the diameter ratio and 16 m/s squares the speed factor again.

items.prompt: A rigid block of volume 0.002 m^3 is held fully submerged in water (1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.81 m/s^2). What is the buoyant force on it?
rubric: Other values come from dropping g or mis-scaling the volume.

items.prompt: Water (1000 kg/m^3) flows through a horizontal pipe whose section speeds up from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. Ignoring friction, by how much does pressure drop?

options.label: 20 kPa
32 kPa
16 kPa
8 kPa

rubric: 8 kPa squares the speed difference, 20 kPa adds squares, 32 kPa omits the half.

items.prompt: Water (1000 kg/m^3, viscosity 0.001 Pa·s) flows at 0.02 m/s in a 0.05 m diameter pipe. What are the Reynolds number and flow regime?

options.label: Re = 10000, turbulent
Re = 1000, laminar
Re = 100, laminar
Re = 1000, turbulent

rubric: Re = rho*v*D/mu = 1000*0.02*0.05/0.001 = 1000, well below about 2300, so laminar.
Distractors mis-compute the arithmetic or misjudge the regime threshold.

items.prompt: Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe of cross-sectional area 0.01 m^2 (water density 1000 kg/m^3). Which values are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Volume flow rate is 0.03 m^3/s
Mass flow rate is 30 kg/s
Mass flow rate is 3 kg/s
Volume flow rate is 30 L/s
Volume flow rate is 0.3 m^3/s

rubric: Q = A*v = 0.03 m^3/s = 30 L/s, and mass flow = rho*Q = 30 kg/s.
Other options are factor-of-ten slips.

items.prompt: A large open water tank has a small hole in its side, 1.8 m below the water surface. The tank stays full, so the surface level is steady. Using g = 9.81 m/s^2 and ignoring friction, what is the speed of the water leaving the hole?

options.label: 35 m/s

rubric: Torricelli from Bernoulli: v = sqrt(2*g*h) = sqrt(2*9.81*1.8) ≈ 5.9 m/s.
4.2 m/s drops the factor of 2; 35 m/s forgets the square root.

items.prompt: Water (1000 kg/m^3) flows steadily through a horizontal pipe at 2 m/s. The pipe narrows to one quarter of its original cross-sectional area. Assuming ideal flow, what is the static pressure drop from the wide section to the narrow section?

options.label: 32 kPa
3 kPa
60 kPa
30 kPa

rubric: Continuity gives 8 m/s, and Bernoulli gives dp = 0.5*1000*(64 - 4) = 30 kPa.
32 kPa ignores the inlet velocity head; 60 kPa drops the factor of 1/2.

items.prompt: A diver is 15 m deep in fresh water (1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.81 m/s^2). Atmospheric pressure at the surface is 101 kPa. What is the absolute pressure at the diver?

options.label: 116 kPa
248 kPa
147 kPa
395 kPa

rubric: Absolute pressure = 101 + rho*g*h = 101 + 147 = 248 kPa.
147 kPa is the gauge pressure only; the others come from arithmetic or conceptual slips.

items.prompt: A solid cube of wood with 0.20 m sides and a mass of 4.8 kg floats upright in fresh water (1000 kg/m^3). How deep is the submerged part of the cube?
rubric: The density is 600 kg/m^3, so 60% of the 0.20 m height is submerged: 0.12 m.
0.08 m uses 40%, which is the fraction above the surface, not below it.

items.prompt: Water (density 1000 kg/m^3, viscosity 0.001 Pa·s) flows at 0.5 m/s in a 0.02 m diameter pipe. What are the Reynolds number and the flow regime?

options.label: Re ≈ 100, which is laminar
Re ≈ 1,000, which is transitional
Re ≈ 10,000, which is turbulent
Re ≈ 10,000, which is laminar

rubric: Re = rho*v*D/mu = 1000*0.5*0.02/0.001 = 10,000, well above about 4000, so turbulent.
Other options mis-scale the number or mismatch the regime with Re.

items.prompt: Laminar flow of oil in a pipe is driven by a fixed pressure drop over a fixed length. The pipe is replaced with one of half the diameter. By what factor does the volumetric flow rate change?
rubric: Hagen-Poiseuille gives Q proportional to D^4, so halving D gives 1/16.
1/4 comes from using area alone; 1/8 and 1/2 come from wrong exponents.

items.prompt: For which of the following can Bernoulli's equation (no loss terms, no shaft work) be applied directly between the two stated points? Select all that apply.

options.label: Steady water flow along a streamline through a short, smooth converging nozzle
Water across a running pump, between the suction and discharge flanges
Water through a 500 m pipe with rough walls, between its inlet and outlet
Low-speed air along a streamline outside the boundary layer ahead of a wing

rubric: Bernoulli holds for steady, nearly inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline: the nozzle and the outer airflow qualify.
Long rough pipes have friction losses and pumps add energy, so the plain equation fails.

items.prompt: A large open tank of water has a 2 cm^2 sharp-edged hole in its side, 4.0 m below the water surface. The tank is kept full, and you may treat the discharge as ideal with g = 9.81 m/s^2. What is the approximate volumetric flow rate through the hole?
rubric: Torricelli gives v = sqrt(2*9.81*4) ≈ 8.86 m/s; Q = v*A = 8.86 * 2e-4 ≈ 1.8 L/s.
8.9 L/s comes from a unit slip with the area; 0.9 L/s drops a factor of 2.

items.prompt: An engineer computes flow rate from the pressure difference across a venturi meter using ideal Bernoulli and continuity. The measured flow is consistently 2 to 5% lower than computed. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Bernoulli's equation ignores gravity, so the pressure difference is overestimated in horizontal pipes
Continuity fails in real fluids, so velocity at the throat is lower than the area ratio predicts
Viscous boundary layers shrink the effective throat area, so the discharge coefficient is below 1
Water is compressible enough that density at the throat is noticeably higher than at the inlet

rubric: Boundary layers and small losses reduce effective flow area, which gives a discharge coefficient below 1.
Continuity always holds for steady flow, and gravity cancels in a horizontal pipe; water compressibility is negligible.

items.prompt: In fully rough turbulent flow, where the friction factor is nearly constant, a water pipeline's flow rate is doubled. By roughly what factor does the friction head loss in the same pipe change?
rubric: Head loss = f(L/D)v^2/2g, so it scales with v^2, giving about 4.
Doubling is the laminar result; larger factors use incorrect exponents.

items.prompt: A pump moves water from a tank at sea level. After it is moved 3 m higher above the water surface, it becomes noisy and vibrates, and the flow drops. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: Atmospheric pressure at the pump rose, compressing the water and making the impeller slip against the casing
The pump now runs in laminar flow, which makes the impeller vibrate at a lower critical Reynolds number
Raising the pump cut the available suction pressure, so local pressure fell below vapour pressure and bubbles formed
Higher elevation increased the water density at the impeller, overloading the blades with extra mass flow

rubric: Greater suction lift lowers NPSH available; pressure at the impeller eye drops below vapour pressure and causes cavitation.
The other options misstate how elevation affects density, flow regime or atmospheric pressure.

items.prompt: A siphon at sea level has its crest 11 m above the upstream water surface, and the outlet is lower than the surface. It will not run, even when primed. Why?

options.label: Atmospheric pressure acts only on the outlet, so a higher crest removes the pressure pushing water over
Gravity acts against flow above 10 m, so the water velocity at the crest drops to zero by Bernoulli
The outlet leg becomes shorter than the inlet leg, so the pressure difference driving flow reverses
Absolute pressure at the crest would have to fall below zero, so the water vaporises near 10 m and the column breaks

rubric: Pressure at the crest is about atmospheric minus rho*g*h, so it drops below vapour pressure before 10.3 m and the column breaks.
The other options misuse Bernoulli, leg lengths or atmospheric action.

items.prompt: A vertical dam face holds water of depth h. The depth doubles. How do the total hydrostatic force per metre of width and its moment about the base change?

options.label: Force ×2, moment ×8
Force ×4, moment ×8
Force ×4, moment ×4
Force ×2, moment ×4

rubric: Force = 0.5*rho*g*h^2 gives ×4; it acts at h/3 above the base, so the moment ∝ h^3 gives ×8.
Other options use a linear force or forget that the lever arm also doubles.

items.prompt: Water flows steadily and without cavitation through a straight pipe of constant diameter that climbs 10 m between points 1 (low) and 2 (high). Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The velocity must drop at point 2 because Bernoulli trades speed for height
The mean velocity at point 2 equals that at point 1 by continuity
The velocity must rise at point 2 because pressure falls with height
The static pressure at point 2 is lower than at point 1

rubric: Constant area and incompressible flow fix the velocity; the pressure falls due to elevation gain and friction.
Bernoulli's trade is between pressure and height here, not speed, since continuity locks the velocity.

items.prompt: A small boat floats in a lake with a heavy steel anchor on board. The crew drops the anchor overboard, and it sinks to the bottom while the boat stays afloat. Compare the lake's overall water level before and after.

options.label: It rises, since the anchor's mass is now added to the water rather than carried above it
It stays the same, since the anchor's weight is still carried by the lake as before
It falls, since the lighter boat rises and the anchor on the bottom is supported by the lakebed alone
It falls, since on board the anchor displaced its weight in water but submerged it displaces only its smaller volume

rubric: On board, the floating system displaces water equal to the anchor's weight; once on the bottom, it displaces only the anchor's volume, which is smaller for steel, so the level falls.
Other options ignore the difference between displacing by weight and displacing by volume.

items.prompt: Water flows through a horizontal venturi meter. The measured pressure drop between inlet and throat is 10 kPa. If the flow rate is doubled with the same fluid, and the discharge coefficient stays constant, what is the new pressure drop?

options.label: 80 kPa
40 kPa
14 kPa
20 kPa

rubric: Pressure drop scales with velocity squared (Q^2), so doubling Q gives 4 times the drop.
Distractors reflect linear scaling (20 kPa), cubic scaling (80 kPa) or a square-root slip (14 kPa).

items.prompt: Laminar flow of oil in a long pipe is driven by a fixed pressure drop. The pipe is replaced by one of the same length but half the diameter. By what factor does the volumetric flow rate change?
rubric: Hagen-Poiseuille gives Q proportional to D^4 at fixed pressure drop, so halving D gives 1/16.
Distractors come from assuming linear, area-based (D^2) or D^3 scaling.

items.prompt: Water leaves a small pipe into a larger pipe through a sudden expansion. An engineer applies Bernoulli's equation without loss terms and predicts a large pressure rise, but the measured rise is much smaller. What best explains the gap?

options.label: Bernoulli's equation only holds in horizontal pipes, and the expansion adds an elevation change to the flow
Flow separation and mixing at the expansion dissipate mechanical energy, so total head falls across it
Water becomes compressible at the expansion because its velocity falls sharply when the pipe widens
Continuity fails at the expansion because the cross-sectional area changes abruptly across that section

rubric: The separated, recirculating flow dissipates energy irreversibly, a loss that the lossless Bernoulli equation omits.
Distractors wrongly blame continuity, compressibility or elevation, all of which are unaffected or irrelevant here.

items.prompt: A sharp-edged hole in the bottom of an open tank drains water. The measured flow is only about 62% of hole area times sqrt(2gh). Which explanation fits best?

options.label: The jet contracts just outside the hole (vena contracta), so the effective flow area is less than the hole area
The falling surface level makes the flow unsteady, so Bernoulli's equation cannot be applied between points
Atmospheric pressure acts on the emerging jet and reduces the pressure difference that drives the flow
Viscous drag in the tank wall boundary layer slows the water by about 40% before it reaches the hole

rubric: Streamlines converge past a sharp edge, so the jet area is smaller than the hole; this is captured by a discharge coefficient near 0.6.
Distractors misattribute the deficit to wall viscosity, atmospheric pressure or unsteadiness, which are minor effects here.

items.prompt: Water flows at Re = 1000 in a smooth pipe. A technician swaps it for a rougher pipe of the same diameter and length at the same flow rate. What happens to the pressure drop?

options.label: It rises in proportion to relative roughness, as in fully rough turbulent pipe flow at high Re
It falls because roughness traps a layer of fluid that lubricates the wall region of the pipe
It stays nearly the same because laminar friction factor 64/Re depends on Re and not on roughness
It rises sharply because the roughness elements trip the flow into turbulence at once

rubric: In laminar flow the friction factor is 64/Re, independent of wall roughness, so the pressure drop barely changes.
Distractors apply turbulent-flow behaviour or imagine roughness always triggers transition.

items.prompt: A centrifugal pump draws water from an open tank and begins to cavitate at its inlet. Which changes would make cavitation more likely? Select all that apply.

options.label: Increasing the flow rate through the suction line
Enlarging the suction pipe diameter at the same flow rate
Raising the pump above the tank water level
Raising the water temperature from 20 C to 60 C

rubric: Higher temperature raises vapour pressure; greater suction lift and higher flow lower the available inlet pressure (NPSH).
A larger suction pipe cuts velocity and friction, which reduces cavitation risk.

items.prompt: A siphon draws water from an open sea-level reservoir over a hump 2 m above the surface, discharging 9 m below it. Ideal Bernoulli gives about -7 kPa absolute at the hump, yet the real siphon flows below the ideal rate and bubbles form at the hump. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The outlet is so far below the surface that its pressure exceeds atmospheric and pushes back on the flow
Dissolved air raises the water density in the hump, so the weight of the descending leg drives less flow
Viscosity at the hump bend turns the flow laminar, which lowers the velocity through the whole siphon line
Pressure at the hump has fallen to the vapour pressure of water, so vapour forms there and limits the flow

rubric: A negative absolute pressure is impossible; the pressure is capped near vapour pressure, so cavitation limits flow.
Distractors invoke laminar transition, density change or outlet backpressure, none of which follow from the numbers.

items.prompt: A water line needs a flow meter. Criteria: accuracy within 1-2% and the lowest permanent pressure loss, because pumping energy is costly; purchase price is secondary. Which device best meets the criteria?

options.label: Venturi meter
Pitot tube at the centreline
Sharp-edged orifice plate
Partly closed valve with a gauge

rubric: A venturi recovers most of the pressure downstream, so permanent loss is low while accuracy stays high.
An orifice plate is cheap but wastes energy; a centreline pitot gives a point value sensitive to the profile.

items.prompt: A junior engineer sizes a pump for a 400 m pipeline with many fittings by applying Bernoulli's equation between two reservoir surfaces with no loss terms. Judge this approach.

options.label: Inadequate, since friction and fitting losses dominate over 400 m, so Darcy-Weisbach and loss coefficients must be added
Acceptable, since the equation is exact for water and the pump head curve will absorb any small error
Acceptable, since flow in long pipes is laminar and losses are negligible next to the elevation difference
Inadequate, since Bernoulli's equation can never be applied between two free surfaces open to the atmosphere

rubric: Over a long run with fittings, head loss is a major part of the required pump head and must be included.
Distractors assume losses are small or misstate where Bernoulli applies.

items.prompt: A 600 m steel pipeline has a pressure wave speed of 1200 m/s. A valve must be closed while limiting surge pressure, and a slower closure is acceptable. Which closure time is best?

options.label: 5 s

rubric: The wave round-trip time is 2L/a = 1 s; closing well beyond it limits the surge pressure.
The shorter times are all faster than the round-trip time, so they give near-full Joukowsky surge.

items.prompt: For fixed flow in a turbulent pipeline, friction head loss scales roughly as D^-5 while pipe cost rises about linearly with D. Which design principle for choosing D is best justified when pumping energy and capital cost both count?

options.label: Choose the diameter where marginal annualised pipe cost equals marginal pumping-energy saving, minimising lifetime cost
Choose the largest available diameter, since friction falls steeply and so total cost always falls with size
Choose the smallest workable diameter, since capital cost is certain while the energy savings are uncertain
Choose the diameter that makes Re just exceed 2300, since laminar flow always has the least friction loss

rubric: Total cost has an interior minimum where the marginal capital cost equals the marginal energy saving.
Extremes ignore one cost term, and the laminar-flow rule misapplies the transition value.

items.prompt: A 1:50 model of a ship hull is tested in a tank to predict wave-making resistance. Criterion: the dominant force balance is inertia versus gravity at the free surface. Which dimensionless group should be matched between model and ship?

options.label: Mach number
Froude number
Weber number
Reynolds number

rubric: Free-surface wave resistance is governed by inertia versus gravity, so Froude similarity is required.
Reynolds, Mach and Weber numbers govern viscous, compressibility and surface-tension effects respectively.

items.prompt: A designer wants to treat low-speed airflow in a ventilation duct as incompressible. Which findings support this assumption? Select all that apply.

options.label: Peak Mach number in the duct is about 0.1
Pressure drop along the duct is about 1% of absolute pressure
Reynolds number is above 10^5
The flow is steady and one-dimensional

rubric: Incompressibility holds when the Mach number is below about 0.3 and density changes from pressure variation are small.
Reynolds number and steadiness do not determine whether density varies.

items.prompt: A designer must choose a surface finish for a 0.1 m sphere moving through air at Reynolds number about 2x10^5, just below the drag crisis. Criterion: minimise drag. A smooth finish is cheap; a lightly roughened finish costs more. Which choice best meets the criterion?

options.label: Roughened, since it trips the boundary layer to turbulence, delaying separation and narrowing the wake
Smooth, since roughness always raises skin friction, which outweighs any other effect on total sphere drag
Either, since at this Reynolds number surface finish has no influence on where the flow separates
Smooth, since a laminar boundary layer stays attached longest and so produces the narrowest possible wake

rubric: Near the drag crisis, a turbulent boundary layer separates later, cutting pressure drag far more than skin friction rises.
Distractors assume that laminar flow stays attached longer or that roughness is irrelevant.

items.prompt: A team estimates pressure drop in a long, smooth pipe by using Bernoulli's equation with the measured velocity and elevation. The predicted drop is far below the measured one. Which critique of the approach is most sound?

options.label: Bernoulli omits irreversible viscous dissipation, so it needs a head-loss term from friction before it can predict a drop in a long pipe
Bernoulli neglects the pipe's elevation change, so the predicted drop is too small whenever the pipe is horizontal
Bernoulli applies only to turbulent flow, so a laminar flow in the pipe invalidates the energy balance entirely
Bernoulli assumes compressible flow, so the density change along the pipe makes the predicted drop too small in a liquid

rubric: Bernoulli is an inviscid energy balance; wall friction dissipates mechanical energy, requiring a head-loss term (Darcy-Weisbach).
Distractors misstate the assumptions: Bernoulli is incompressible, includes elevation, and is not limited to turbulence.

items.prompt: For pumping a viscous oil through a long pipe at fixed flow rate, a designer compares increasing the diameter by 20% versus doubling the pump size. Criteria: minimise operating energy, flow is laminar. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Enlarge the pump: in laminar flow the pressure drop is independent of diameter, so only pump capacity matters for energy
Enlarge the pipe: in laminar flow the pressure drop scales as 1/D^4, so a 20% increase cuts it by about half
Enlarge the pipe: in laminar flow the pressure drop scales as 1/D^2, so a 20% increase cuts it by about 30%
Enlarge the pump: laminar friction rises with velocity squared, so pump power is the dominant lever on energy cost

rubric: Hagen-Poiseuille gives dP proportional to Q/D^4; 1.2^4 is about 2.07, so the drop halves.
Distractors use the wrong exponent or turbulent scaling (velocity squared) for laminar flow.

items.prompt: A venturi meter is used to measure flow of a liquid. An engineer proposes ignoring the discharge coefficient because Bernoulli is exact for a smooth converging section. Which evaluation is most defensible?

options.label: Accept: continuity fixes the velocity ratio exactly, so the coefficient only matters if the fluid is compressible at all
Reject: Bernoulli cannot be applied across a contraction, so the coefficient replaces the energy equation altogether in the meter
Reject: boundary layers and small losses make the real flow slightly lower than ideal, so a coefficient near 0.98 corrects the inviscid estimate
Accept: a smooth contraction conserves energy exactly, so any measured discrepancy must come from the pressure taps alone

rubric: Real venturis have viscous boundary layers and minor losses; the coefficient (about 0.95-0.99) corrects the ideal flow.
Distractors wrongly claim Bernoulli is inapplicable or exact, or tie the coefficient to compressibility.

items.prompt: A tall rectangular gate holds back water. Criteria: minimise the moment about the hinge at the gate's base for a given water depth h. A colleague uses the resultant force acting at mid-depth. Which critique is correct?

options.label: The resultant acts at h/3 below the surface, so mid-depth overestimates the moment about the base for a vertical gate
The resultant acts at the centre of pressure, 2h/3 below the surface for a full-height vertical gate, so mid-depth underestimates the lever arm error
The resultant acts at the centroid, so mid-depth is right and the moment is simply rho g h/2 times area times h/3 everywhere
The resultant depends on gate material density, so no location can be stated without knowing the gate weight at all

rubric: Pressure grows with depth, so the resultant is below the centroid, at 2h/3 from the surface (h/3 above the base).
Distractors confuse centroid with centre of pressure or misplace it.

items.prompt: Two designs for a water supply line are compared at the same flow: A has a sudden contraction to a smaller pipe; B uses a gradual taper. Criteria: lowest head loss and least risk of cavitation downstream. Which is best justified?

options.label: A, because a sudden contraction raises velocity sharply, which raises local pressure and suppresses cavitation downstream
B, because gradual tapers reduce separation and vena contracta losses; a sudden contraction creates low-pressure zones that raise cavitation risk
B, because tapers lower the flow velocity at the throat, which is why they have lower friction than any sudden change
A, because separation zones recover pressure efficiently and so lower the total head loss relative to a taper

rubric: A sudden contraction causes a vena contracta with low local pressure and extra loss; a taper avoids separation.
Distractors reverse the velocity-pressure relationship or claim separation recovers pressure.

items.prompt: An engineer judges whether Bernoulli's equation can be applied between two points on a streamline for a real system. Which conditions must hold for the simple form to be reasonably accurate? Select all that apply.

options.label: No pump or turbine lies between the points
Flow is steady along the streamline
Viscous losses between the points are negligible
Density is approximately constant

rubric: Simple Bernoulli needs steady, incompressible, effectively inviscid flow along a streamline.
A pump or turbine can be included by adding a head term, so its absence is not strictly required.

items.prompt: A harbour engineer must choose a fender float. A steel-hulled barge of mass 40 t is loaded to a draft where it just floats in fresh water. It will move into estuary water of higher density. The engineer judges the effect on draft and on metacentric stability margin. Which assessment is best?

options.label: Draft increases because denser water pushes up less per volume, so freeboard shrinks and stability margin necessarily improves
Draft decreases because less volume is needed to displace the same weight; the stability must be rechecked since the waterplane properties and centre of buoyancy shift
Draft decreases, so the barge floats higher and its stability is guaranteed to fall because the displaced mass drops
Draft is unchanged because the weight is the same, so the buoyant force and the metacentre are unchanged

rubric: Buoyant force equals weight; denser fluid needs less displaced volume, so draft falls, and the stability must be reassessed.
Distractors reverse density effects or assume unchanged geometry or guaranteed stability change.

items.prompt: Design a siphon to drain a tank over a 3 m high ridge using water at 20 C. Constraints: the pressure at the highest point must stay above vapour pressure (about 2.3 kPa abs), atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa, and losses are small. Which ridge height above the free surface meets the constraints?

options.label: Up to about 20 m, because atmospheric pressure supports a taller water column than the vacuum limit
Below about 9.8 m of rise above the free surface, less the velocity head, so a 3 m rise is feasible with margin
Any height, because a siphon works through gravity and cannot be limited by vapour pressure
Only below 1 m, because the lowest pressure always equals the pressure at the outlet minus friction

rubric: Atmospheric pressure supports about 10 m of water; subtracting vapour pressure and velocity head still leaves a 3 m rise feasible.
Distractors ignore cavitation or misstate the theoretical column limit.

items.prompt: You must design a flow-metering section for a gas line with Mach number near 0.4 at the throat. Constraints: error under 1% and a simple orifice or venturi. Which design choice meets every constraint?

options.label: Include an expansion factor for compressibility in the flow equation, since density changes across the throat at this Mach number
Choke the throat deliberately, because a Mach 1 throat makes the flow independent of downstream density changes
Use the incompressible equation unchanged, since Mach 0.4 is far below the speed of sound
Use the incompressible equation with a doubled discharge coefficient to absorb all density changes

rubric: At Mach about 0.4, density changes of several percent exceed a 1% error budget, so an expansion factor is needed.
Distractors ignore compressibility, hide it in the coefficient, or choke needlessly.

items.prompt: Design a lab test to find whether a flow is dynamically similar to a full-scale ship hull moving in water. Constraints: the dominant force balance is gravity versus inertia, and the model is 1/25 scale. Which test matches?

options.label: Match the Reynolds number, so model speed is full-scale speed multiplied by 25
Match the Froude number, so model speed is full-scale speed divided by 25
Match the Mach number, so model speed equals full-scale speed in the same fluid
Match the Froude number, so model speed is full-scale speed divided by 5

rubric: Froude similarity gives V proportional to sqrt(L), so speed scales as 1/5 for a 1/25 model.
Distractors choose the wrong dimensionless group or mis-scale the square root.

items.prompt: Design a pipe network upgrade. Constraints: a parallel pipe is added to an existing line so the total flow rises, and both pipes have the same end pressures. Which statement about the design is correct?

options.label: The head loss across each parallel branch is equal, so flow divides by each branch's resistance and total flow is the sum
The head loss adds across the branches, so the total loss equals the sum of both and flow falls
The flow in each parallel branch is equal, so the added pipe always carries half of the total flow
The pressure drop in the added pipe is zero, because the existing line already sets the end pressures

rubric: Parallel branches share the same head difference; flows sum and split by resistance.
Distractors confuse series and parallel rules or assume an equal split.

items.prompt: A pump must lift water from a sump to a tank. To avoid cavitation, design the suction side. Constraints: available NPSH must exceed the required NPSH by a margin. Which modification raises the available NPSH?

options.label: Lower the pump nearer the sump level and shorten or enlarge the suction line to cut friction
Narrow the suction pipe so the velocity head rises and the margin increases
Raise the pump well above the sump to give a larger static suction lift
Warm the water to lower viscosity, which raises its vapour pressure margin

rubric: NPSH available rises with lower static lift and lower suction losses.
Distractors worsen lift, raise velocity losses, or ignore that warmer water raises vapour pressure.

items.prompt: Design a model test of flow in a pipe to predict full-scale pressure drop. Constraints: viscous forces dominate, the fluid is incompressible, and the model is smaller than the prototype. Which conditions are needed for similarity? Select all that apply.

options.label: Match the Reynolds number
Match the pressure coefficient in advance, as an input
Use geometrically similar models, including relative roughness
Match the Froude number as well, since gravity always matters in pipes

rubric: Pipe flow similarity requires geometric similarity (including relative roughness) and Reynolds number matching.
Froude matters only with free surfaces; pressure coefficient is the output, not an input.

items.prompt: A designer wants a small hydraulic jack to lift 10 kN using a hand force of at most 200 N. The hand piston has area 2 cm^2. Constraints: incompressible fluid, negligible friction, and a lift piston not larger than 120 cm^2. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: A lift piston of about 100 cm^2, since the area ratio of 50 gives 200 N times 50 equal to 10 kN
A lift piston of about 50 cm^2, since the force is the hand force times the diameter ratio
A lift piston of about 200 cm^2, since force equals pressure times the larger area at all times
A lift piston of about 10 cm^2, since a smaller piston gives a larger multiplied force

rubric: Pascal's law: F2/F1 equals A2/A1, so 10 kN/200 N is 50, giving 100 cm^2, within the limit.
Distractors invert the ratio, exceed the size limit, or use diameter instead of area.
